speechtext:
At any rate the Canadian
government guaranteed this loan and the banks, acting in their ordinary capacity as banks, simply carried out a regular transaction with a government guarantee. The banks advanced the money required to complete this purchase. Nine of these ships were delivered. They were not all of the same type. Some of them were specially made Yangtze river boats which are specially designed to operate in the shallower waters of the Yangtze river. The others were regular cargo vessels, and of course these cargo vessels would seek to do business in other waters. Apparently the Yangtze boats are able to operate to Hong Kong, or so it would appear because in the publication issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce known as "Foreign Trade", under date of June 16, 1951, there is this news report:
Hong Kong-Canton passenger service resumed.
Hong Kong, June 1, 1951.- (FTS)-On May 21, ;he S.S. Chien Men, a Canadian built river vessel belonging to the Ming Sung Industrial Company, departed on the first trip signalling the resumption of regular passenger service between Hong Kong and Canton. Although the Ming Sung vessels have been running a weekly service to Canton via Macao, and ferrying Malayan-Chinese repatriates to the mainland, for several months, this sailing of the Chien Men marked the first resumption of direct scheduled Hong Kong-Canton service since the latter port was occupied by the Chinese communists almost two years ago. The new service will operate three times a week, leaving Hong Kong every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.
That raises two points. One is the arrangements under which the Chien Men, under Canadian registry, is able to operate satisfactorily into a communist controlled port. The other is what is meant by the reference to the repatriation of Malayan-Chinese to the mainland. So far as I know, the only mainland to which these repatriates could be delivered is the mainland of communist China. I think the house should be informed whether this is taking place under some agreement with the international Red Cross, whether it is the repatriation of wounded prisoners of war, or whether this is a restoration to Chinese soil of those who were engaged in any activity which left them outside their home lands. Ordinarily it is essential that there be very exact information as to the reason for affording safe conduct to people back to a soil from which armed men come to engage in battling those who go from Canada to the battle line on which the people of both these nations are now engaged.
When the minister says that this was an ordinary transaction, he no doubt has
Ming Sung Industrial Company reference to its being an ordinary transaction of the nature that is carried out when the government has full and arbitrary, powers which 'are exercised without the ordinary supervision of parliament. He also doubtless refers to the sort of things that could be done under emergency legislation, because these contracts were carried out under the special authority given the government at that time.
This contract was carried out by highly reputable companies; but one company did raise a special problem. That was George T. Davie and Sons Limited of Levis, Quebec, which had been operating for some time. Unfortunately the president, Mr. Davie, met his death in a tragic automobile accident. It then became necessary for the government to intervene, and the Canadian Commercial Corporation had some responsibilities in that regard. In that connection I might say this company was shown to have been incorporated on November 26, 1941, with an authorized capital of 2,500 shares. The president was Andre Delagrave of Quebec city; the secretary was Maurice Paquet of Lauzon; a director was Brenda Delagrave of Quebec city, and the solicitors were St. Laurent, Gagne and Tasehereau of Quebec city. This company continued to operate and was the subject of the special arrangements, which have not yet been fully disclosed, through the agency of the Canadian Commercial Corporation. As a result of the combined activities that were carried out, the contracts were fulfilled.
The next important stage in these proceedings after these ships were delivered follows as a result of the occupation of the Chinese mainland by the communist government which is now in power. As a result of that an application was made for the incorporation of the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada Limited, which company was incorporated on March 13, 1950. I have not the permanent board of directors, but the provisional board of directors are shown in the record; and the solicitors filing the application were Duquet and MacKay of Montreal. That company was organized to take over the ownership of these ships now operating in the China sea, from Hong Kong to Macao to Canton, in the circumstances indicated.
An interesting point is that the head office of the company is shown as Charlottetown. However, inquiry by telephone in Charlottetown produced the report that the telephone company has not heard of this company, which has no telephone number there. What operations are being carried on in Canada by the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada

Ming Sung Industrial Company
Limited of course are not yet disclosed, other than the operation of these ships in that area. Another' interesting point is that when an inquiry was made as to the activities of the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada Limited, apparently it was necessary to direct that inquiry to Hong Kong. While this is a Canadian company, evidently that was the place where the information could be obtained. And the information obtained there, such as it was, came from another subsidiary, the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Hong Kong Limited. So we see this combined picture of the company operating in communist China: the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Hong Kong Limited and the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada Limited, both taking the best possible advantage of the best of all possible worlds. Undoubtedly this is a very satisfactory transaction from the point of view of the company operating in the communist area and the company operating in Hong Kong and the company which has the advantage of a Canadian flag and exemption from the ordinary provisions of Canadian law.
Then when we come to the directorate of the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada Limited, these are the officers, though I certainly do not guarantee the pronunciation: Directors, Tso-Fu Lu, Hong Kong; Tomas S. J. Wang, Montreal; Chen-Chi Yang, Hong Kong; Shong-Sung Tong, Hong Kong; Y. C. James Yen, New York; R. G. Peers, Montreal, vice-president; R. D. MacKay, Montreal, secretary-treasurer. This is the company which now operates the service that has been -described.
Undoubtedly it would be a matter of interest to learn whether the statements contained in the message received by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) had yet been fully checked. I submit that the only statements contained in the letter which came from Hong Kong and which has been placed before this house which have not been fully proved are, first, the statement that there is a Russian captain in charge of one ship and, second, that munitions of war are being carried. It has been agreed by the government that this change of registry did take place last spring. The government have stated that they are aware trade is going on with Macao; and it is very interesting that the trade with Macao apparently began just after the Korean hostilities opened. At that time, of course, there would be obvious reasons which need not be explored, since they are self-explanatory, why certain facilities would be afforded at Macao which might not be available at Hong Kong, no matter how wide open the provisions were there at that time, .and the provisions were sufficiently wide

open to call for criticism in the British House of Commons. That criticism has continued and has led to the announcement in London today by Sir Hartley Shawcross to which I have just referred. The government was fully informed in regard to the details of this transaction and in regard to the change of registry. There is an order in council dated Tuesday, May 16, 1950, which fully sets out the original arrangements for the construction of the ships, the advance of the money by the banks, the terms under which repayment was to be guaranteed, and also the setting up of the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada Limited. So the setting up of this Canadian subsidiary of the company which operates in communist China was not merely an ordinary commercial operation; it was fully approved and recognized, by the government in that order in council. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that instead of reading this order in council to the house in full it be placed on Hansard associated with today's recorded debate. Otherwise I shall be called upon to read it in full, since it sets forth the full details of this transaction.

Assistant Clerk of the Privy Council
The text of this order in council indicates that the government contemplated the transfer of these ships to the Ming Sung Industrial Company. I shall read a short extract from part of it to indicate the knowledge of the government at that time. It reads:
since the date of the execution of the said supplementary agreement, the Chinese company has proposed that it will sell and transfer to Ming Sung

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Ming Sung Industrial Company Industrial Company of Canada Limited, a company incorporated under the Companies Act (Canada), hereinafter called "the Canadian company," seven of the said ships or vessels (now said to be in or near Hong Kong) and that they shall then be transferred to Canadian registry under the Canada Shipping Act and that the Canadian company shall execute and deliver a mortgage or mortgages thereof in form registerable in Canada in favour of the Chinese company for the amount of the purchase price, namely, $12,750,000 . . ,
That is all I intend to quote at that point. It will be seen that by this order in council the government not only indicated its acceptance of the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada Limited as the company to which these ships were to be transferred by a Chinese company operating in communist China, but in that very order in council it also provided for the registration of these ships under Canadian registry.
We then have this situation confronting us. The ships were sold. They were operated by the Ming Sung Industrial Company Limited, with head offices in communist China. It obviously became impractical for that company to operate these ships in waters where such naval vessels as were posted by the government of Chiang Kai-shek were operating, and whatever the purpose was, protection to operate in that area was accorded these ships by this transfer to Canadian registry and the transfer to a Canadian company with head offices in Charlottetown. These ships are not operating .under Canadian masters, nor are they operating under masters who are British subjects. They are operating with Chinese crews, and they are operating into a communist controlled port. They are operating out of Hong Kong into Macao. The invitation of the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Hong Kong to examine the manifestos of these ships is meaningless as any evidence of security, because those ships can go to Macao, unload everything they have and then take on board a load of contraband which could be delivered to communist China.
I urge, Mr. Speaker, that when these facts are presented it shall not be suggested there is any implication that this government was consciously aiding an enemy in the receipt of supplies. On the other hand, we must examine the facts as they are. I submit that the unchallenged facts, completely ignoring the question as to whether there is a Russian captain-I must say that I do not know that a Chinese communist is any better than a Russian communist-the fact remains that the evidence is clear, with what we already know, that these ships have been accorded special privileges which would make it possible for them to carry materials that would assist the enemy, at a time when that enemy

is sending its troops to fight our troops in Korea. I am not splitting words. I say "the enemy". The Chinese who are firing rifles and artillery weapons and manning the aircraft, if they are, which are attacking our men in Korea today, are Chinese sent by the Chinese government. We must act with full recognition of the reality of that grim truth.
Recognizing that truth, and with the sordid history of trading with the enemy under disguises of various kinds in the past, I suggest that this house would simply be carrying out the obvious course dictated by common sense and respect for the dignity of our flag if the special exemption accorded by this government to the Ming Sung Company and those ships were immediately withdrawn. For the reasons I have stated, and so that the house may be in a position to indicate its views simply related to that one act, which would be fully effective, I am presenting a resolution calling for the withdrawal of that exemption. In case anyone may say: But that deals only with the exemptions, may I point out that immediately the exemption is withdrawn these ships cannot operate any longer under the Canadian flag. The resolution is therefore drawn with a recognition of that fact.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that the exemption granted under section 133A of the Canada Shipping Act by the Minister of Transport on May 12, 1950, to the seven ships or vessels owned by the Ming Sung Industrial Company of Canada Limited and registered under the Canada Shipping Act should be immediately withdrawn.

I believe that this is at least the
fourth occasion, Mr. Speaker, when this matter of the operation of these ships built in Canada, and still of Canadian registry but now operating out of Hong Kong, has been discussed. I quite appreciate the interest hon. members have in the assertions that were contained in a circular letter addressed by a gentleman from Hong Kong on June 4 to certain members of this house, and to certain newspapers. We had heard from our trade commissioner that this letter was coming forward, and before the matter came up here I can give the house the assurance that I was as much concerned as any hon. member of this house has been since the matter was raised here.
I do not think it would be boasting for me to assert that I would deprecate as much as any person in this house anything that could

render more difficult the task of those brave young Canadians who are supporting the cause of the United Nations in Korea at this time, and who are having such distinguished, if you will, but dangerous military operations to conduct against personnel, including large numbers of Chinese soldiers, who are there, without its being possible to cast the least doubt upon it, with the authority of the present government of the mainland of China. Because this charge was a serious matter and was so regarded, it was gone into extremely carefully. I should now like to make a rather full statement of the manner in which the whole incident has arisen.
It will be remembered'-and I do not think I will be contradicting any of the facts asserted by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), although I think they will perhaps appear in a somewhat different light when the circumstances are taken into account- it will be remembered that these ships were a part of a certain number of ships that were being built here in Canada for foreign purchasers immediately after the cessation of hostilities. It will also be remembered that there was great anxiety in many quarters in Canada about the possibility of serious unemployment developing here after the cessation of the activities that had been so magnificent, so outstanding, during the war production period. At that time parliament, on the recommendation of the government of which I was a member, authorized loans to foreign governments for the purpose of enabling them to place contracts with Canadian firms. Some of those contracts were placed with firms in Canada, one of the firms being this firm at Lauzon, George T. Davie & Sons, Ltd., to which the hon. member referred as having at the time as its president one Andre Delagrave. The hon. member perhaps did not know that Andre Delagrave was the brother-in-law of the late Mr. Davie who had died in this automobile accident, and that he took that position in order to protect the interests of the Davie family. The lady mentioned-I am not quite sure of the name but I think it was Brenda Delagrave-	-

In any event, the lady mentioned was the member of the Davie family that Mr. Delagrave had married and whose interests he was seeking to protect. That is, of course, neither here nor there. It is just a fact that explains how it was that George T. Davie & Sons, Limited, had as its president Andre Delagrave.
Ming Sung Industrial Company
These ships were built, and I understand that a good job of work was done and that they were put out in an extremely workmanlike manner for the special conditions of the trade in which they were to engage. At that time the arrangement that was made was that fifteen per cent would be provided in United States dollars-and United States dollars were not plentiful anywhere-by the purchaser who would borrow the rest from Canadian banks and would take an export credit insurance policy under the set-up that was established by this parliament for the purpose of enabling foreign buyers to provide work in Canadian plants. Then there was the guarantee of the government of China, but that was not regarded by our banks as sufficient, any more than was the guarantee of the government of France or the government of several other countries whose citizens were placing orders in this country. It was for that purpose, and because of that necessity, that parliament set up this export credit insurance scheme.
The ships were later transferred by this Ming Sung company, a Chinese company, to a company established in Canada which, as the hon. gentleman has said, had its head office in Charlottetown. Anyone who has had any experience over the last twenty years in the practice of law and in having to advise foreigners who were setting up companies in Canada knows why Charlottetown was frequently selected as the place to have the head office of a company. Before I came here I advised1 on the incorporation of a great many companies that had their head offices in Charlottetown, and I think there were offices there which were simultaneously the head offices of tens of different companies. That feature presented nothing surprising to anyone who had been familiar with the practice which was due to the fact that provincial corporation taxes were less onerous there than they were in some other jurisdictions.
The ships were transferred from the Chinese company to this company incorporated in Canada but having Chinese nationals as a majority of its directors. But that again was nothing surprising. All hon. members of this house who are lawyers know that it quite frequently happens that there are set up for clients residing abroad Canadian companies which have one, two or three Canadian directors but whose real directors, those who control the policy, are non-residents of Canada. The ships were transferred from the Chinese company to this Canadian company, and a mortgage on the ships was given to the Chinese company and transferred by the Chinese company to

Ming Sung Industrial Company the banks as additional security. This Ming Sung company is a trading company that, from the information we had been able to secure, has been in existence for a long time and has a variety of trading interests in Asia. According to the information we got, it is a company that has always lived up to its contractual obligations and has always taken care of its debts as they mature. As a matter of fact, that is what has been done up to the present time with regard to the construction costs of all these ships.
We felt that it was desirable to make as secure as could reasonably be done the claim of the Canadian banks against the owners of the ships. In order to enable that to be done these ships were exempted from certain provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. The hon. gentleman inquires how it happens that in the list of exemptions that was tabled on the 1st of February this special one was not indicated. Well, that list is a tabulation made by the director of nautical services from the reports, or from the files, that come from various inspection districts, of which there are seven or eight throughout Canada. There is one in Vancouver, one in Quebec, one in Saint John and there are several of these steamship inspection offices to whom the owners of a ship which is not able to comply with all the requirements of the act make application for an exemption. A great many of these exemptions are granted throughout the year.
The director of the nautical services made up from his files a list of the exemptions that had been granted, and that is the list which was tabled in this house as sessional paper 124A-2 on February 1, 1951. How does it happen that he did not put this other one in? He did not put the other one in because it did not come through the ordinary channel of the district inspectors' offices.
This is something out of the ordinary. We have not a steamship inspector in Hong Kong, and there are not very many Canadian ships that are operating in foreign waters. There were not a very large number of ships built in Canada for the foreign trade.
This is a matter which had been handled here in Ottawa. I inquired, as the leader of the opposition is inquiring, why was this not in the list. It was not in the list because there was no file in that collection of files dealing with it, and as a matter of fact it is not required to be tabled until the end of this year. But it is true to state that it was not tabled at the very beginning of this session. The information about it is available and will be tabled almost at once.
Here I simply wish to make the statement that I was just as much concerned as anyone can be, and that I am satisfied so far

that what has been done was done properly, though I would be happier if this exemption had been included in the ordinary list. There was no desire to withhold anything. There had been another exemption under another section of the Canada Shipping Act, section 406, I think, which is covered by an order in council passed on May 5.
These ships-we are talking about five now-were exempted, all seven of them, from the requirements of carrying radio operators. That was done by the order in council which names the ships, and which was tabled-it was passed on May 5, and was included in the monthly summary of orders in council tabled on June 14. In any event, it was disclosed at once because it was felt that it was the proper thing to do. Now, it may be that it will turn out it was not the wise thing to do, but at the time everyone would have considered that it was the proper thing to do. It was a method that was being taken to protect, in so far as we felt it reasonable to protect, the claims of the banks for the amounts they advanced, and to protect the Canadian taxpayer against the effect of the guarantee which had been issued under this insurance scheme of export credits.
Some days before the matter was raised in the house we received information from the trade commissioner that this circular letter, or something of that kind, was going forward, and was going to the newspapers. The trade commissioner said that he was going to check because the information was from a biased source, namely the China Coast Navigating and Engineer Officers' Guild, which was not too happy over the fact that any British ship was being allowed to operate without having its personnel of officers and engineers British subjects. It was a trade situation that was displeasing to the guild of China coast navigating and engineer officers, because it allowed Chinese subjects to take jobs which otherwise would have been exclusively reserved to British subjects; the commissioner said he was going to check the assertions that were made. When the matter was first raised in the house the explanation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was that he was waiting for further information in that regard.
Well, now, the information we have up to the present time-we have not yet received positive information about what goes out of Macao, which is a Portuguese port, but the information we have with respect to Hong Kong is that nothing goes out of there that is on the list of embargoed commodities of the United Kingdom and its crown colonies.

There are things which are on our embargo list, which we do not allow to be exported from Canada to China, but we felt that if ships were operating on the high seas it would not be proper for us to determine what should be the policy of the port of a friendly nation, an allied nation, a commonwealth nation, with respect to commodities that it would allow to go to communist Chinese territory.
We feel that the government of the United Kingdom., the people of the United Kingdom, would be just as much concerned if there were materials under their control going to China that could be of any help to the Chinese against British soldiers who are fighting side by side with our sons in Korea. We think that we are not the only holy people in the world, and that there are others who have the .same reaction to humanitarian and patriotic consideration that we have, and that it is proper for us to say what Canadian commodities will not be exported out of Canada to China, but that it is proper for the government of Hong Kong, the government of the United Kingdom in its crown colony of Hong Kong, to say what it considers can be exported out of Hong Kong toward China, without endangering the safety of the soldiers from the United Kingdom who are fighting alongside men from others of the United Nations in Korea.
With respect to Macao, Macao is a Portuguese port. Portugal is one of our allies in the Norih Atlantic treaty arrangement. 1 would imagine that though Portugal is not a member of the United Nations, because by the veto of the Soviet representative it has been kept out, it would be quite as much concerned as are we about support or comfort given to this aggression in Korea, because the North Atlantic treaty was formed for the very purpose of protecting North Atlantic countries against aggression. We think that by discouraging this aggression in Korea we are likely to be able to prevent aggression elsewhere. Because that is our position we are risking a great many Canadian lives and spending a great many millions of Canadian dollars.
Until we have evidence to the contrary, we think it is fair to assume that the Portuguese authorities at Macao "would no more than the British authorities at Hong Kong willingly allow contraband to be carried by these ships into Chinese territory.

I did not want to interrupt the Prime Minister, but just so that he may help us in understanding this will he state why, if there is such confidence in what is

speechtext: I would not call a blacklist a list of countries for which export permits have to be obtained. I should not like it to go from this house that the attitude of the Canadian parliament is that our Portuguese allies under the North Atlantic treaty are on our blacklist. I do not think that that would be helpful.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: A. M. HILL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, just a moment; Macao is quite different from Portugal proper. Macao is included in the list of these areas to which I have just referred, not Portugal or Portuguese possessions. It is the specific port of Macao that is mentioned, for reasons which I think the Prime Minister understands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: A. M. HILL
speechtext:
The reason for this list is that we consider it preferable that no strategic materials get into that area. That is our view. We think that no strategic materials from Canada should get into that area. It may very well be that there would be no legitimate trade in them, but there is always the possibility of contraband. Though we on this side of the house do not agree with certain generals of our great allies south of the border that there should be a blockade of China, we do feel that all reasonable precautions should be taken to keep out of that area at this time such strategic materials as may be useful elsewhere. It is for that reason that exports to certain Asiatic countries cannot be made without permits.
The payments to the banks on these Chinese ships have always been regularly made, but that would not be a weighty consideration if in our opinion there were any serious grounds for thinking that the continuation of what is being done would in any way endanger any of our Canadian young men on the peninsula of Korea. That is being checked just as carefully as possible.
The hon. gentleman says, "You can tie up these ships by withdrawing the exemptions which you have granted." Probably that could be done. I imagine that the manner in which the Ming Sung Company has always conducted its operations would make it comply with any regulation that was effective in Hong Kong. Without transferring the registry of these ships to some other country they certainly could not operate with Chinese officers if these exemptions were withdrawn. I do not think that that should be undertaken lightly. I do not think it would be fair to the Canadian taxpayer to put him in the position of having to make good this guarantee unless there is more to suggest the possibility of wrongdoing than this circular letter from

Ming Sung Industrial Company a source which our trade commissioner describes as being biased. That does not mean it is dishonest, but one knows how easily rumours can get started and how easily they can be propagated.
I have not yet felt that our responsibility- I take it as seriously as any member in this house-to the men we are sending to Korea requires us to take that step without further evidence that there was more than a possibility of there being contraband carried to this area. The fact that we have certain commodities that we do not allow to go to China but which up to the present time have not been prohibited from shipment out of Hong Kong does not in my view justify us in withdrawing these exemptions which have been accorded. I think it would be an indirect attempt to say to the United Kingdom government that we think they have been or are being unwise in the kind of commodities that they allow to be loaded on ships trading out of that port.
All hon. members know that the British and the Americans, or some of the Americans, have not seen eye to eye as to the proper policy or the extent of applying restrictive policies to trade with China. Some people believe that there should be an armed blockade of China preventing all kinds of trade and traffic with that country. There are several hundred million Chinese in that territory, there are several hundred million in the other Asiatic countries, and I think it would be a sorry state for the western world if all those human beings were driven permanently into the communist camp. The policy that this government and our Department of External Affairs have been trying to follow is to bring about some kind of negotiated settlement of the Korean incident in the hope that it will not become necessary permanently to treat as belonging to the iron curtain part of the world those great Asiatic populations.
These are our views which are just as honestly entertained as are entertained the views of some of the citizens of our great American ally who think that there should be at once a complete naval blockade of China. I do not doubt the honesty of such views, though I do doubt their wisdom. In this regard, what has been done up to the present time by this government with respect to these ships is what I think any government from any party in this house would have done up to this time. Whether another government made up from another party in this house would at this time withdraw the exemptions that have been accorded I am unable to say. I do not think they would. From what we have been able to ascertain through these sources up to the


present time I think it would be unwise to withdraw these exemptions and thus brand the owners of these ships as unreliable. If we branded them as unreliable and put them in the position where they cannot operate, it would be natural for them to say, "Well, you will just have to wait for your money". That again would not be enough to stop us from acting if there were any serious indication that harm to the cause of the United Nations and our men in Korea was being occasioned by the operations of these ships. But we must not lose our perspective. There is no doubt that Chinese troops are engaged in the operations in Korea, but there are between 400 million and 500 million people in China, and it is by tens of thousands that those who are engaged in warlike operations have up to the present time been counted. The rest of China is living; the rest of China is carrying on some part of its normal life; and X think there is justification for what has been up to the present time the view of the British government that it would be unwise to cut off trade in non-war commodities between Hong Kong and the mainland of China.
As to the ferrying operations to which the leader of the opposition referred, I am not in a position to give any information. Hon. members will realize that we do not attempt to put inspectors on these ships to see what they are doing. It is my understanding that Malaya is the place where Mr. Malcolm MacDonald is the governor. It may be that he would feel there are some Chinese Malayans or Malayan-Chinese whom he would like to see back on the mainland just as we would be quite happy to see anyone ferrying some who are here in Canada at the present time and to whom we would bid bon voyage if they were leaving to go back behind the iron curtain. That is one possibility. I do not know whether or not that is the real explanation, but I would not be surprised if the former high commissioner to Canada would perhaps feel that it would make his situation more comfortable if there were fewer of 'those who have any desire to go back to the mainland of China remaining under his government.
The hon. member referred to a press dispatch in which Sir Hartley Shawcross was said to have stated that the list of embargoed commodities out of Hong Kong to the mainland of China was going to be increased. We would welcome that. We have not the same opportunities for knowing the situation as have members of the United Kingdom government, but if they were to adopt the list of commodities that we have said will not be exported from Canada to China we

would be inclined to feel that it was at least confirming the wisdom of our selection. On the whole I prefer to believe that it would not be wise for us to adopt, vis-a-vis our partners in the North Atlantic treaty alliance, a holier-than-thou attitude.

speechtext: Nor was anything that I said suggestive of a blockade, nor did anything that I said indicate that we were taking any action in relation to the Chinese government, no matter what we think of it. maintopic: A. M. HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that this house is of the opinion that the exemption granted under section 133A of the Canada Shipping Act should be removed from the seven vessels owned by the Ming Sung Industrial Company, there are certain points that I should like to bring to the attention of the house which I think emphasize the importance of taking action now and not delaying until further reports may be gathered. I suggest there is sufficient evidence at the present time to justify withdrawing the exemption. I am not surprised that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) admitted concern over these very unfortunate circumstances that have arisen in connection with this trade. I am sure that we are all concerned about this matter because it may directly influence the course of the operations in which our troops are taking part in Korea at the present time.
Far from being any holier-than-thou attitude, the leader of the opposition was merely recommending taking reasonable precautions against the firm operating these vessels under the Canadian flag. The Prime Minister referred to the fact that this matter had been before the house on four occasions. The previous occasions were when the house was in committee of supply dealing with various estimates, and hon. members may not have had the opportunity then of expressing their opinions as to the correctness of the course recommended in the
Ming Sung Industrial Company amendment. Considerable emphasis has been laid upon the fact that the letter i received from Hong Kong was sent to other people. The letter was addressed to me personally. I can hardly call it a circular letter. I did not know that anybody else had received it when I first raised the matter.
It was stated that those who had sent the letter were biased. They are vitally concerned with the matter being a guild or union of responsible ships' officers who have been employed in the navigating and engineering services of vessels plying in the China seas. I am prepared to accept their opinion just as readily as I will accept the opinion voiced by the Chinese officials of this Chinese company who, I must also point out, would be equally biased. This morning I rose before orders of the day were called to point out that I had received' a cable from Hong Kong this morning in which confirmation was given of the statements that had been made in the letter. This certainly is not a circular letter; it is a cable addressed to me at the House of Commons, Ottawa: Reference Canadian flagged vessels trading locally. Confirm strategic cargoes loaded Macao for Canton.
It is signed by the China coast guild. There is confirmation of the statements previously made in the circular letter of June 4. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) referred to the fact that the Ming Sung Industrial Company were always able to take care of their debts. Well, at the present moment they are engaged in a very lucrative trade. The fact that this trade is lucrative is borne out by figures in the last edition of Foreign Trade, published under the authority of the foreign trade service of the Department of Trade and Commerce, under date of June 16, 1951. These figures show the increase in trade between Hong Kong and various countries in the first quarter of this year over a similar period a year ago. At page 1066 under the caption "Hong Kong trade is largest with China" we find this statement:
Trading returns for the first quarter of 1951 reveal significant changes in the relative importance of Hong Kong's traditional partners, when compared with returns for the same period in 1950. The following table, in terms of millions of Hong Kong dollars, indicates alterations in the proportion of the colony's trade enjoyed by certain countries.
The table shows China and in brackets "including Macao"; and it is rather significant that Macao should be linked so definitely with China here. In the first quarter of 1951 the total trade with China is given as 1,028 million Hong Kong dollars, and the percentage of the total trade is 35-7. For the first quarter of 1950 the total -trade with China including Macao was 512 million Hong Kong dollars, so in the last twelve months the trade has doubled. I am not going to quote figures for
4312

Ming Sung Industrial Company the other countries mentioned, but the final note of this paragraph is also rather interesting:
It is noticeable that trade with the United States, usually Hong Kong's second most important trading partner, has declined by 40 per cent. The drop is directly related to that country's embargo against China, and its rigid control over export shipments to Hong Kong.
When one considers that this Chinese company is carrying on a major share of the trade between Hong Kong, Macao, Canton and China, and that this trade has doubled in the past twelve months, it should be well able to take care of the interest on this debt, which was originally some $12 million.
It has been stated that this company has been trading in China for a long time. It has been pointed out that the headquarters of the company are listed as being at Chungking, China, with branches at a number of Chinese ports including Shanghai, Tsingtao, and so forth. Undoubtedly this company operates in accordance with the instructions given it by the Chinese government. It could never carry on its activities all through red China unless it adhered to those instructions; and I do not suppose there is the slightest doubt but that the Chinese government makes a very good thing out of the activities of this company. No doubt the ordinary taxes would be imposed; and I think it is a pretty well known fact that in addition the handouts given by trading companies to Chinese governments of the past have been on a pretty generous scale.
Another point of interest, which I think should emphasize the necessity of taking action now, is this transfer or repatriation of Chinese communists from other parts of Asia. It will be recalled that in the letter read to the house on June 15 by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, addressed to the Hong Kong representative of the government by Mr. C. C. Yang, a member of the Ming Sung Industrial Company, he gave the routes being followed by the various vessels:
Our vessels in trade: Hong Kong-Macao, passenger and cargo; Hong Kong-Macao-Canton, passenger and cargo; Hong Kong-Canton, passenger only; Hong Kong-Canton (nonscheduled service).
Overseas Chinese sent back to China from Malaya, Indonesia and sometimes cargo.
It is rather a coincidence that in the Associated Press dispatches coming from Singapore last Monday we are told:
Glittering promises and come-back-to-China groups are luring hundreds of wide-eyed Chinese students from Singapore to communist China.
The prospect of becoming leaders of the masses . . . is held out to the youngster. Police have located undercover rings specializing in this work	
[Mr. Pearkes.l
The situation was dramatized by the pick-up in Hong Kong recently of six Chinese school girls from prominent families ....
Propaganda cells work in schools and social organizations that glorify red China, police said. At the same time, alluring letters from students already in China are bait for new converts.
So that when you read that in conjunction with the report from Foreign Trade read by the leader of the opposition, in which it mentioned that one of these vessels the Chien Men is carrying Malayan Chinese repatriates to the mainland of China, it is quite obvious the type of the repatriate who is being taken back. No one would be so naive as to think that communist China would permit anything but communists to return to China. Canton has been in the hands of the Chinese government now for the past two years.
There is one other point which I wish to bring out, and that is in connection with the statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) when he was giving the reasons for granting the exemption. On page 4172 of Hansard for June 15 this statement is made:
It was also stated that there were no British officers, mates or engineers available, and that the only officers, mates and engineers available were those of Chinese nationality.
This was referring to the time the exemption was given, which was in April of 1950. It is rather difficult to reconcile that statement with the statements which were being made in the spring of 1950 by the Minister of Transport, who was pointing out that it had become necessary to reduce the Canadian merchant marine. Many ships were being sold out of the Canadian flag, and a policy was being adopted of reducing the number of vessels we had to little more than a skeleton fleet. On page 2236 of Hansard for May 5, 1950, the Minister of Transport made the following statement in speaking on his estimates:
In passing, however, I might remind the house that Canadian costs of operation are about double British costs, and in order to maintain the Canadian shipping industry it was decided to permit owners to transfer to United Kingdom flag.
A little later he said:
At the time of such statement there were 174 Canadian owned ocean-going vessels. Two were sold since that date . . . transfers to United Kingdom flag have been approved in respect of 93 ships, and transfers in respect of 23 ships are still pending.
It will be recalled that the government policy announced about that time was that a subsidy would be given to maintain a fleet of Canadian-owned ships, I think it was about 40 vessels. This was a large reduction from the 200 odd merchant vessels we had during the war. In order to encourage merchant seamen to find other occupations, the Minister of Veterans Affairs at that time

introduced a system of extending vocational training courses to members of the merchant marine. Surely that indicates that there was no dearth of Canadian seamen at the time this exemption was being granted. The minister has not told us what steps he took to find out whether or not there were Canadian or British officers, mates and engineers available. I wonder whether he relied entirely on the word which had been given, no doubt by the Ming Sung Company.
With these facts before us, the fact that even now there should be no shortage of Canadian seamen available and anxious to find employment, the fact that it has been proven beyond doubt that material which may easily be of strategical value to the enemy is passed by these ships into communist held ports, the fact that there is a movement of Chinese communists from other ports in Asia being transported by these vessels into communist China, who may be used as leaders in various walks of life and perhaps in the armed forces which are now in operation against our own men, I feel that there is no time to be lost. It would be an exceedingly wise precaution to withdraw this exemption from these vessels now. The Canadian banks and Canadians may suffer financially a little bit. It used to be considered that $12 million was a large sum, but I do not think that $12 million is so huge a sum that it could not be taken care of by the government if the government felt it was in any way obliged to refund that amount of money.
I repeat what I said the other day. I believe Canadians would rather lose that money than think that that money was derived by possibly helping the enemy. The evidence seems to me to be so clear that I repeat I think it would be a wise course to suspend the operations of these vessels by withdrawing the exemption which was granted. For these reasons, I am supporting the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition.

maintopic: A. M. HILL
speechtext:
There was one feature of the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) this afternoon which caused me great concern, and that was the fact that he seemed to place so little importance on the manner in which Canada gave these ships the privilege of using her flag. The Canadian merchant marine has a proud record. We have a very good Canada Shipping Act, designed for supervising the operations of that merchant marine. Yet if actions of this kind are taken to any extent, that Canadian registry will be in danger of being classified in the same way as we now class Panamanian registry. The Prime Minister knows that many ships were placed 80709-274a
Ming Sung Industrial Company under the flag of Panama under conditions which certainly did not lead to an increase in the respect for that flag.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has not dealt particularly with this section 133A of the Canada Shipping Act. If he will refer to it I am convinced that, being the great lawyer he is, he will realize that that section was never designed for a use such as that to which it has been put in this present case.
The section provides that the Minister of Transport may grant exemption from the provisions of four other sections of the Canada Shipping Act. One of those four sections contains the requirement that there must be a certified master and other deck officers; a second requires that there must be certified engineers; a third provides for the production of the master's certificate when he wants to get a clearance from the customs authorities in the various ports; and the fourth section has to do with clearance for a coastal trip. In respect of each one of those provisions it obviously was intended to provide for exempting a ship where no danger to that ship would follow. For example, the last half of this section 133A reads that the minister may grant these exemptions
... if he is satisfied that that requirement has been substantially complied with in the case of that ship, or that compliance with the requirement is unnecessary in the circumstances of the case, and that the action taken or provision made as respects the subject matter of the requirement in the case of the ship is as effective as actual compliance with the requirement.	.
In other words, this section 133A is merely meant to provide that the minister may grant an exemption where, for example, the ship will be in no danger if an officer holding a certificate not up to the standard is in charge on that particular trip. That fact is confirmed by this list of exemptions which was tabled' by the Minister of Transport early in the present session. Most of the exemption^ dealing with officers of the ships provide for the carrying of a master with an inferior licence. There are a few which provide for the carrying of a master who has not a certificate, and I think there are two dealing with mates who have an inferior certificate. Then there are exemptions for engineers, chief engineers, second engineers and so on. That is the kind of exemption which was provided for by this section 133A.
There was never any intention that it should be used to enable Chinese ships or ships of any other nation to use the Canadian flag. I do not believe it was contemplated by a Canadian parliament that there would be action taken of this kind under which seven ships belonging to China have been allowed to use the Canadian flgg. In effect,

Ming Sling Industrial Company they have been given a wholesale exemption. The result of the exemption given is that Canada has said: "Here, you can use our flag; and as long as you pay back this money, we do not care what else happens." I can see that the reason for that action was to make the repayment of the money more certain. But it is breaking down the Canadian shipping [DOT]laws and taking away the value of the Canadian flag on a merchant ship.
While this fact that the ships are trading with communist China is to me a serious matter-ana I do not want to leave the impression that it is not

the other serious factor, and the one which appeals to me, is *that we have allowed the Canadian flag to be used in this way.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that he could get over the difficulty by allowing this company to register its ships in Hong Kong. Let them go under the merchant shipping act. If that is done, there can be from Hong Kong a direct control over the ships, a much better control than we can exercise from Ottawa. If, as the Prime Minister says, the owners of these ships are reliable businessmen, surely that would not endanger the amount of money that the Canadian government has tied up in this deal. The businesslike way to handle the situation now would certainly seem to be to get these ships transferred from the Canadian registry. They are *not Canadian ships. There is no reason at all why they should be classed as Canadian ships. The only thing Canadian about them is that they were built here; and they were put under Canadian registry for a purpose which was never contemplated under the Canada Shipping Act.
I urge upon the Prime Minister that he give consideration to having the ships transferred to the registry in Hong Kong, and in that way seeing to it that they no longer use the Canadian flag. Even if they have not already got into trouble, even if they have not already done things which have hurt the reputation of this nation, they are apt to do something like that in the days that lie ahead. There is still war going on in Asia. The Chinese government is still fighting the United Nations' forces in Korea. Sooner or later the fact that these ships are carrying a Canadian flag may bring great discredit to our nation. I urge upon the Prime Minister that steps be taken to have the ships transferred from the Canadian registry.

maintopic: A. M. HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to add just a word to what has been said. There were two things said by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to which I wish to advert briefly. First of all,
IMr. Green.]
although the Prime Minister did not make a great point of it, he spoke of the money side; he spoke about the getting back of the money as being one of the reasons against taking the action suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). On that matter I just wish to say this. At the present time we are presumably spending millions of dollars every month in Korea for the purpose of protecting the lives of our own men; and it seems to me that if there is any appreciable risk of any added danger, we should not take that risk.
The second thing, and the one that I wished to stress more particularly was this. The Prime Minister seemed to suggest or rather he in fact suggested-and with considerable seriousness-that to take the action proposed, which after all is merely to withdraw a privilege which has been given, might really permanently turn against us the minds of hundreds of millions of Chinese not only in China but throughout the world. If that were true, it would of course be a dreadful and alarming thing. But I suggest to the Prime Minister that actually infinitely more serious things than that are happening at the moment. As he has said, we are actually fighting the Chinese in Korea. We are killing them and, alas, they are killing us. Therefore the suggestion that this withdrawal of a privilege from half a dozen ships, which I suggest 99-9 per cent of the Chinese throughout the world will never hear of, might prejudice our relations with those people to an extent even comparable with the prejudice which comes from the fact that we are now fighting them, is one that I confess I find to be extremely unconvincing.

The branches of this department are the mines branch, the geological survey of Canada, the surveys and mapping branch, the geographical branch and the dominion observatories. The functions of these branches may be described briefly as follows:	The mines branch undertakes in
its laboratories the analysis of ores and minerals of economic interest, metallic, nonmetallic, radioactive and fuels, their production, processing, utilization and marketing, the investigation of metals and alloys and their properties and uses. The information thus secured is made available to the mining and metallurgical industries of Canada with a view to stimulating the production, use and export of the country's mineral wealth.
The geological survey of Canada carries on geological studies in the field and office designed to promote the discovery and development of Canada's mineral resources. The results of investigations are made available to prospectors and other interested parties in the form of geological maps and reports. It also carries on surveys using the recently developed airborne magnetometer. The branch provides, free of charge, identification of mineral specimens submitted by prospectors and the general public, and checks samples for radioactivity.
The surveys and mapping branch is made up of five divisions. They are as follows: Topographical survey, Canadian hydrographic service, geodetic survey of Canada, legal surveys and aeronautical charts, and map compilation and reproduction. Their main functions are as follows: The topographical survey division is the primary mapping organization of the federal government, and is responsible for topographical mapping on scales of four miles to one inch and larger, from both ground and air surveys. It carries out the surveys for the control of air photography, details topography from both ground surveys and air photographs, and prepares the resulting maps to the manuscript stage.
The Canadian hydrographic service is responsible for the charting of the coastal and inland waters of Canada, and for the study of the water levels on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence waterway. It carries out hydrographic surveys and investigations,
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys and publishes charts, sailing directions, tide tables and other results of its work.
The geodetic survey of Canada provides a national system of precise triangulation. and level control on which are based detailed topographical, hydrographic and other surveys. It provides control for air surveys inremote areas by means of astronomical fixations. The geodetic survey is currently co-operating with the national research council and the Royal Canadian Air Force in the development of shoran apparatus, and techniques designed to obtain geodetic measurements from aircraft.
The legal surveys and aeronautical charts unit carries out surveys of dominion land under the direction of the surveyor general. It is also responsible for the preparation of air navigation charts used in the "Canada Air Pilot", and for this purpose plots air photographs on scales smaller than four miles to one inch. It maintains a central distribution office for all maps prepared in the surveys and mapping branch.
The map compilation and reproduction division is the division which is responsible for the drafting of the maps produced by all divisions of the surveys and mapping branch, and for the printing of both maps and charts. To carry out this function it has specialized compiling, drafting, photographic and lithographic units.
The geographical branch is a comparatively new one, having been organized in 1947 with-the objective of collecting and making available geographical data on Canada and foreign countries for the use of government and other interested organizations. It is currently engaged in the preparation of an atlas of Canada, and the compilation of geographical data on strategic areas ii)t northern Canada and on the east and west coasts.
So far as the dominion observatories are concerned, the main observatories are located at Ottawa and Victoria, B.C. They are responsible for scientific studies in stellar and solar physics, in terrestrial magnetism, ingravity and seismology. From Ottawa Canadian standard time is broadcast over station? CHU for the benefit of surveyors, aerial navigators and ocean shipping.

Thirty-six are completed and some survey work only is completed on the balance. We have one geologist on the dam sites that the hon. member has mentioned.

speechtext:

.* Mr. Adamson: I should like to ask the minister a question about the water levels on the great lakes. At the present time the water levels particularly of lake Ontario and Surrounding waters are abnormally high. It is generally considered that they follow a certain cyclical trend. We used to call it the old seven year cycle or seven year sine. Three or four years of abnormally high water have rather upset all previous calculations, and it is causing a great deal of damage to the shore line. I should like the minister to say whether the geodetic survey has made any study of the level of the waters of the great lakes, and I would ask him whether he has any statement to make on the abnormally high water level which has persisted for a number of years.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: This department has taken levels through the hydrographic survey branch and has made the information available. That is as far as our responsibility goes.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Is nothing done about runoffs? Is nothing done about the flow of


rivers? Is nothing done about the flow of the Niagara river and the St. Lawrence river?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I believe that comes under the water and power bureau of the Department of Resources and Development.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That brings up the next question. Where does the Department of Resources and Development stop and where does the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys start? Where is the division of authority between the two?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: This is a technical department only; we do not do any development work. We carry out survey projects for other departments.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That was the policy of the old department of mines; they did not do any development work. I remember the survey and prospecting parties going into the field, and the one thing they were afraid of was that they might find an ore deposit. I assume the minister is equally hopeful that they do not find anything of commercial value. All they want to do is chart the geology of the country. With respect to the geological survey, would the minister say how many parties are out this year, where they are; who is the chief of the geological survey branch and if possible who are the chiefs of the various parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I think we can give that information when we come to the particular item if that would be satisfactory.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That is perfectly satisfactory. Now I should like to ask a question with regard to the air survey. Would the minister say how much of the dominion has been mapped and what is the program for the coming year with regard to topographical mapping through the air survey? At the same time could he explain the "Canada Air Pilot", whether it is on a route basis or an area basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: The department tries to photograph from the air about 200,000 square miles a year. For the actual topographical mapping survey work we have about sixty parties in the field.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That is, as distinct from the geological survey, there are sixty mapping parties? Are these all airborne, and how many personnel would be in this group?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: The average party consists of five or six persons, and they are usually transported to the remote areas by air and then left to do their survey work on foot.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: It is the old method of triangulation and ground survey; it is not done by aerial photography?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: These survey parties establish control points which can be related to the aerial maps.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I would be interested to learn how much of the country is being mapped, because I realize there is a tremendous job to be done in mapping the country both topographically and geologically. In Canada we have pioneered in air mapping, and I wonder if the minister could say how much has been mapped, what is the furthest boundary north, how much it is expected will be done this year, whether we are mapping north of the tree line yet, whether we are mapping in the Northwest Territories, whether we are dealing with specific things such as river basins, and in short a general statement. I appreciate that the topographical mapping of the country presents the department with a tremendous job and I would like the minister to explain what is being done.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: A great deal of topographical work has been carried out in the northern reaches of the Cariboo, some of it in co-operation with the Americans in Alaska. In our own district the work of photographing from the air is well in advance of anything the United States is carrying out on its side of the line. I happen to know that from conversation with some of the surveyors and I thought it would be of interest to hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Practically all Canada to the remote north has been photographed and mapped by the trimetrogon system. They are now proceeding to photograph it by vertical photography, and relating it to the control points established by these topographical parties. About two-thirds of the photography by the second method has been completed.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Has it been carried on north of the boundaries of the three prairie provinces? Have those provinces been mapped?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: The trimetrogon work has all been done.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Those maps are available?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: They are available at eight miles to the inch only.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: There are no maps at four miles to the inch or one mile to the inch for that territory?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Not yet.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Has the air force helped in that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
The air force has been doing a great deal of that work. This year of necessity they have had to curtail their activity,
Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys and for that reason we are having to engage more private companies to do it.

speechtext: Order. Since hon. members began putting questions to the minister on mapping, topographical surveys and so on, I have been examining the estimates. maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN

speechtext:
Under this item would the
minister explain what facilities his department has in Ottawa? Some of the most efficient methods now being used in connection with our present mining development were developed by our scientists and engineers and chemists and physicists here in Ottawa, and I should like to know whether the ore dressing laboratories and other facilities of the old department are now under this department or whether they are under the Department of Resources and Development? speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
That all comes under this
department now. We have the mineral processing division, the industrial minerals division, the fuels division, the physical metallurgy division and the minerals resources division.

speechtext: Under this heading, might I ask if there is any intention of reviving a provincial-dominion arrangement whereby trails and transportation facilities are opened up into new property? inch?

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I should like to advise the minister that I am interested in the Lloyd-minster oilfield. I notice that in the sessional committee on railways and shipping owned and operated by the government, on Tuesday April 17, 1951, Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways was asked whether that heavy type of oil in the Lloyd-minster field is suitable for use in locomotives. Mr. Gordon's answer is as follows:
Bunker C oil is used in our oil-burning locomotives; but diesel oil is used in our diesel operations. In western Canada our operations are almost entirely oil-burning. In fact, west of Edmonton we operate entirely with a converted type of oilburning locomotive in which we use bunker C oil. I might say that we are concerned about the supply of bunker C oil and we would like to see a very much greater development at the Lloydminster field.
I should like to ask the minister if this is the department that might assist in the further development of that field, as this oil is so necessary for the use of the oil-burning locomotives.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
This vote provides for the purchase of capital equipment items for use in the laboratories and machine shops, and for replacement of motor vehicles.
Construction of a new machine shop and stores building is well advanced, and it will be occupied during this fiscal year. A large part of the machine tool equipment in use in the old shop is obsolete and incapable of doing fine work to the close tolerances required for development of metals for defence purposes. Lack of space in the old shop prevented the purchase and installation of any new equipment. With the additional space and improved facilities provided by the new building, it will be possible to instal new, modern lathes, shapers, milling machines, grinders, et cetera and $50,000 has been requested for this purpose.
An amount of $242,000 has been included for the purchase of scientific apparatus and machinery for use in the laboratories, and ore dressing and metallurgical mills. Approximately $136,000 of this amount is a revote for equipment for which funds were provided in 1950-51 but which was not delivered in that year. The balance is for new equipment for research on improved ore dressing and metallurgical processes in connection with strategic minerals and metals for defence purposes.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: On many occasions I have been asked what happens when a prospector brings a piece of radioactive ore to the department. I have had several complaints that they did not seem to be particularly interested. A prospector may have a sample of ore from a deposit which he may or may not have staked. He gets a geiger counter reaction from the ore but is interested in finding out from the department how much uranium oxide thei'e is in the sample. The percentage of uranium oxide in the ore indicates its value; it does not matter what reaction you get on the geiger counter. What is the procedure when a sample of ore is brought in to the department? What happens? And how is the prospector or developer informed about the value of the ore so brought in?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
When a sample is sent in it is given a geiger counter assay and the percentage of radioactive material is determined. This usually takes about a day. If the

hon. gentleman knows someone who has been brushed off I should like to know about it and have the hon. gentleman tell him to come around again.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
They were not particularly
interested in stating whether there was a geiger counter reaction. You could probably get a radioactive reaction from a geiger counter in this chamber. It is the percentage of uranium oxide that is of value. Does the department make a report giving the percentage of uranium oxide? Does the department say:	We have received the
sample, we have assayed it, it has a certain percentage of uranium oxide in it, and we think you had better go out and stake the deposit? Or does the department say: This is a valuable deposit and we think you should turn it over to the Eldorado Mining and Refining Corporation? I should like to find that out because the development of radioactive ores and uranium oxide is one of the most important we can carry on at the present time in Canada.
It is not particularly attractive commercially. There is only one buyer. There is a set price, and it is not a simple thing for the average prospector to discover. He gets a reaction on a geiger counter and he says: I have a deposit of uranium. Frequently he has not, but the decision whether he has or has not is one that the department, through technical officers, can make for him, or at least tell him whether he should go on. I should like to know what happens when a man brings in a sample of ore. I know the geiger counter readings and I know what happens, but what I am interested in is whether the department tells him it is a certain type of rock, what he should look for, and advises him how to continue the development of a potential property.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Both thorium and uranium
are radioactive, and to have a complete analysis of a sample there would have to be a chemical analysis which would take longer. That would be done by the mines branch if it was thought the sample warranted that amount of work. It can be told by preliminary tests whether it is rich enough for chemical analysis. Chemical analysis can take as long as a month to complete, but that is done whenever the specimen warrants it.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Can the minister say what
percentage of uranium oxide they consider valuable?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys

0-50 per cent or more.

An order in council was
passed on November 4, 1950, authorizing the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to enter into an agreement with McGill university under which the university will be reimbursed for its costs in developing a coal-fired gas turbine in an amount not exceeding $125,000. At the present time I understand the project is still on the drawing board and they are not quite ready to start the actual construction of the experimental model.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
This information has
already been released to the press. The geological survey has eighty-eight parties in the field. Assessment of strategic minerals including tungsten, molybdenum, chromite and antimony, which are essential to Canada's defence program, will form an important part of this year's program of the geological survey. The work is to include further examination and mapping of the Quebec-Labrador iron region, mapping of areas believed to be favourable for the occurrence of oil, gas and coal, and examination of uranium-bearing deposits. The staff of the regional office established in Calgary last year will examine a great number of drill cores and cuttings available in that area to aid in the interpretation of the stratigraphy of the oil fields. Examination of glacial deposits including gravel, clay and sand, and the study of the ground water resources, will be extended to include the important industrial areas of Montreal and Vancouver. A special detailed study of the Sydney coal fields of Nova Scotia will be continued as an aid to the industry in planning further development of coal deposits. Parties have been arranged as follows:

speechtext:

speechtext: I was interested and pleased, I may say, to see that the department is doing so much work in connection with our ground water resources. I assume it is preparing water tables of certain areas of Canada. Having in mind the chronic water shortage in large areas of the United States, has the minister any information on the extent of the ground water resources and the lowering of the water tables in the prairie provinces and in southwestern Ontario? Is this condition general, and is the department in any way concerned over the destruction of our essential ground water resources?

speechtext: I know that the province is doing that work. As a matter of fact, I have some friends actually engaged in the ground water surveys at the present time. Is any information available? maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
That is exactly the information which I believe the country should have before we reach the stage of a chronic lack of water. What does the department intend to recommend? Where are the districts which are already showing shortages of

Supply-Mines and Technical Surveys ground water? Has the government, through the department, any suggestions for the preservation of this source of life? Large areas in the world have been destroyed through the destruction of the ground water reserves. I do not think anything could be more important than this work that the department is doing.

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Can the minister tell me whether any surveys have been made in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: In relation to water?

maintopic: THE UKRAINIAN CATHOLIC EPISCOPAL CORPORATION OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Yes.
